title: Did, doing, will — without changing the verb
title_target: แล้ว กำลัง จะ — Láaeo, kam-lang, jà
goal: Place actions in time using small words around the verb — the part of Thai that brings the most relief to anyone who has ever memorized European verb tables.
bekal: using จะ for the future
using กำลัง…อยู่ for things in progress
using แล้ว for things that have already happened
telling ยัง…อยู่ (still) apart from ยังไม่ (not yet)
answering …หรือยัง questions correctly

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — A midday phone call
dialogs.intro: Nok calls Budi. In this dialogue the verbs *ไป*, *กิน*, *ทำ* appear again and again in different times — and not one of them changes form. Only the words around them change.

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [ฮัลโหล|Han-lǒo] [พี่|phîi][บูดี|Buu-dii] [ตอนนี้|tawn-níi][ทำ|tham][อะไร|à-rai][อยู่|yùu][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Hello, Phi Budi. What are you up to right now?
lines.literal: hello — older-sibling — Budi — right-now — do — what — (ongoing) — (polite)?

lines.text: [กำลัง|Kam-lang][กิน|kin][ข้าว|khâao][อยู่|yùu][ครับ|khráp] [มี|Mii][อะไร|à-rai][เหรอ|rǒoe][ครับ|khráp]

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [พรุ่งนี้|Phrûng-níi][จะ|jà][ไป|pai][เชียงใหม่|Chiang-mài][ใช่|châi][ไหม|mǎi][คะ|khá] [จอง|Jaawng][ตั๋ว|tǔa][แล้ว|láaeo][หรือ|rǔue][ยัง|yang][คะ|khá]

lines.literal: tomorrow — will — go — Chiang-Mai — correct — (question) — (polite)? book — ticket — already — or — yet — (polite)?

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [จอง|Jaawng][แล้ว|láaeo][ครับ|khráp] [แต่|Tàae][ยัง|yang][ไม่|mâi][ได้|dâai][จอง|jaawng][โรงแรม|roong-raaem][ครับ|khráp]

lines.literal: book — already — (polite). but — still — not — get-to — book — hotel — (polite).

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [รีบ|Rîip][จอง|jaawng][นะ|ná][คะ|khá] [ช่วง|Chûang][นี้|níi][คน|khon][เยอะ|yóe][ค่ะ|khâ]

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [เดี๋ยว|Dǐao][เย็น|yen][นี้|níi][จะ|jà][จอง|jaawng][ครับ|khráp] [น้อง|Náwng][นก|Nók][เคย|khoei][ไป|pai][ไหม|mǎi][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: I'll book it this evening. Nong Nok, have you ever been?
lines.literal: in-a-moment — evening — this — will — book — (polite). younger-sibling — Nok — ever — go — (question) — (polite)?

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [เคย|Khoei][ค่ะ|khâ] [ไป|Pai][มา|maa][เมื่อ|mûea][ปี|pii][ที่แล้ว|thîi-láaeo][ค่ะ|khâ] [เพิ่ง|Phôeng][กลับ|klàp][มา|maa][ตอน|tawn][ปีใหม่|pii-mài][ด้วย|dûai][ค่ะ|khâ]

lines.literal: ever — (polite). go — come — when — year — last — (polite). just — return — come — at — new-year — also — (polite).

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [แล้ว|Láaeo][ยัง|yang][อยาก|yàak][ไป|pai][อีก|ìik][ไหม|mǎi][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: So do you still want to go again?

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [อยาก|Yàak][ค่ะ|khâ] [แต่|Tàae][ยัง|yang][ไม่|mâi][ว่าง|wâang][ค่ะ|khâ] [เดือน|Duuean][หน้า|nâa][ค่อย|khâwy][ไป|pai][ค่ะ|khâ]
lines.id: I do. But I'm not free yet. Maybe next month.
lines.literal: want — (polite). but — still — not — free — (polite). month — next — only-then — go — (polite).

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [งั้น|Ngán] [ผม|phǒm][ถ่าย|thàai][รูป|rûup][มา|maa][ให้|hâi][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: Then I'll take some photos for you.
lines.literal: in-that-case — I — take — picture — come — for — (polite).

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [ขอบคุณ|Khàwp-khun][ค่ะ|khâ] [เที่ยว|Thîao][ให้|hâi][สนุก|sà-nùk][นะ|ná][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Thank you. Have a great trip!

notes: **Thai verbs NEVER change form.** *ไป* means go, went, is going, and will go — all of them. What sets the time is the small word around it, or even just a time expression at the start of the sentence. This is the best news a language book can deliver.

**And often even the marker isn't needed.** *เมื่อวานไปตลาด* (yesterday went to the market) is complete with no marker at all, because *เมื่อวาน* already says it all. Thai speakers use markers only when the time isn't clear from context.
**จะ jà = will, and it goes BEFORE the verb.** *พรุ่งนี้จะไป* (tomorrow will go). It's also used for a decision just made: *เดี๋ยวจะจอง* (I'll book it in a bit).

**กำลัง…อยู่ wraps around the verb and means "in the middle of".** *กำลังกินข้าวอยู่* (eating right now). Either one can be used alone: *กำลังกิน* or *กินอยู่* are both correct and both common. Using both together sounds most natural.

**แล้ว láaeo = already, and it goes at the END of the sentence.** *กินแล้ว* (have eaten), *ถึงแล้ว* (have arrived). ⚠️ Don't be tempted to put it in front of the verb the way English puts "already"; its place is always after.

**ยัง…อยู่ = still; ยังไม่ = not yet.** Note the difference: *ยังกินอยู่* (still eating) and *ยังไม่กิน* (haven't eaten yet). The single word *ไม่* changes the whole meaning, and you'll hear both all the time.
**เพิ่ง phôeng = just.** *เพิ่งกลับมา* (just got back). It goes before the verb and often pairs with *เมื่อกี้ mûea-kîi* (a moment ago).
**ค่อย khâwy here means "later, then".** *เดือนหน้าค่อยไป* = I'll go next month instead. This is different from *ไม่ค่อย mâi khâwy* (not very) that you met in unit 6 — watch for the *ไม่* in front.

grammars.title: The entire Thai time system in one table
body: The verb used throughout this table is the same: *กิน kin* (eat). Notice that it doesn't change a single letter.

กำลังกินอยู่
ยัง + verb + อยู่

after: ⚠️ **Watch the different positions:** *จะ, กำลัง, ยัง, เคย, เพิ่ง, ไม่* all go **before** the verb; *แล้ว* and *อยู่* go **after**. If in doubt, remember one thing: **แล้ว always goes at the end.**

grammars.title: …หรือยัง and how to answer it
body: The question "…yet or not?" is one of the most frequent patterns in everyday Thai conversation, and its answers have set forms worth memorizing.

head: Question
Pronunciation
"Yes, already"
"Not yet"
rows: กินข้าวหรือยัง
ยัง / ยังไม่ได้กิน
ถึงหรือยัง
จองหรือยัง
ยังไม่ได้จอง
แต่งงานหรือยัง
พร้อมหรือยัง

after: **ยังไม่ได้ + verb means "haven't gotten around to it"** — slightly different from plain *ยังไม่*, "not yet". *ยังไม่ได้จอง* implies the intention is there but hasn't happened; *ยังไม่จอง* is more neutral. The difference is subtle and won't trip you up — but *ยังไม่ได้* is the form you'll hear most.
⚠️ **Answering a …หรือยัง question with just ครับ/ค่ะ isn't enough**, a habit English speakers carry over from "yes". Answer by repeating the verb: *กินแล้วครับ* or *ยังครับ*.

sections.title: ไป and มา: two verbs that attach everywhere

blocks.text: *ไป pai* (go) and *มา maa* (come) aren't just ordinary verbs. Both often attach **after** other verbs to show the direction of the action — away from the speaker, or toward the speaker.

blocks.title: ไปไหนมา — a greeting that isn't a question
items: *ไปไหนมา pai nǎi maa* literally means "went where and came back?", and it's the most common everyday greeting between neighbors and coworkers — much like "where have you been?" said in passing.

It does **not** demand an honest or detailed answer. The standard, perfectly polite reply is just a few words: *ไปตลาดมาครับ/ค่ะ* (been to the market) or even simply *ไปธุระมาครับ/ค่ะ pai thú-rá maa* (had some errands).
⚠️ Don't answer it with a long explanation. That only confuses the other person — they're greeting you, not questioning you.

sections.title: Time expressions that save you markers

blocks.text: Because verbs don't change, time expressions carry the whole load. The good news: their position is free — at the start or end of the sentence.

blocks.text: An example that shows the whole idea of this unit at once: *เมื่อวานไปเชียงใหม่ วันนี้กลับมาแล้ว พรุ่งนี้จะไปทำงานครับ* — yesterday I went to Chiang Mai, today I'm back, tomorrow I'll go to work. Three different times, three verbs that don't change at all.
